Medieval Drama. Emerged from the church's need to make scripture vivid and memorable to illiterate congregations. Beginning as simple liturgical interpolations, dialogue and action added to the mass, it evolved into elaborate musical-theatrical spectacles performed in the nave and marketplace. By the late Middle Ages, secular drama including mystery cycles and morality plays dominated, yet retained music as essential. Chant, polyphony, and instrumental music carried dramatic weight and spiritual resonance in ways words alone could not.

Liturgical drama originated in the tenth century, likely at Saint Gallen monastery, as conversations sung between clergy at Christmas and Easter services. The Quem Quaeritis trope, a brief dialogue asking Whom do you seek? between angels and the three Marys, is the first documented medieval drama.

Hildegard of Bingen composed the Ordo Virtutum, around eleven fifty-one, an elaborate morality play featuring polyphonic singing and staging. It is one of the earliest known compositions by a named woman. Mystery cycles, including York, Chester, and Towneley, were massive multi-day theatrical events retelling biblical history with music, spectacle, and popular humor.

Morality plays like Everyman presented allegorical characters such as Greed, Death, and Good Deeds engaging in moral instruction through dramatic dialogue and music.

Music in medieval drama served practical purposes. It cued emotional tone, maintained pace, and provided acoustic separation between scenes. The boundary between religious and secular drama blurred. Comedic, tragic, and allegorical plays all incorporated music and performance.

Hildegard of Bingen is a pioneering composer of liturgical drama whose Ordo Virtutum stands as a surviving masterpiece. Everyman is a celebrated morality play representing the mature form of medieval allegorical drama. The morality play is the secular derivative of liturgical drama emphasizing ethical instruction. Liturgical music is the musical foundation from which medieval drama emerged. Gregorian chant is the monophonic basis for early liturgical dramatic interpolations. Polyphony is the harmonic technique that elevated later medieval drama's musical sophistication.
